title: Food is life
hook: giving food gives life, beauty, happiness and strength

segments.voice: Yesterday: removing grudges, five tools, and your line, grudge removed. Today, a gift that's easy to give without noticing.

A Koliyan town called Sajjanela. A laywoman named Suppavasa has invited the Buddha to her house for a meal, and she serves him with her own hands, good food, until he's had enough. Scenes like this come up again and again in the suttas: a lay household inviting the Buddha for a meal. But this time, after the meal, the Buddha doesn't just thank her. He tells her what she has actually given, and it turns out a plate of rice is a bigger gift than it looks.
screen: `A LAYWOMAN NAMED SUPPAVASA.` → `SHE SERVES WITH HER OWN HANDS.` → `WHAT DID SHE REALLY GIVE?`

segments.voice: When a woman disciple gives food, the Buddha tells Suppavasa, she gives four things to the one who receives it. She gives life. She gives beauty. She gives happiness. She gives strength. Take that literally. Without food, there's no life. Food puts color back in a pale face. A good meal after a long day is happiness you can taste. And it's what lets the body walk, work and sit in meditation. Then the surprise. Having given life, beauty, happiness and strength, the Buddha says, she herself will share in all four, whether among humans or among the gods. The gift goes out and comes back. This is how the early texts think about giving, dana. It isn't only a moral duty or a fee for teaching. It's a circle: the monk couldn't survive without the householder's food, and the householder's giving becomes part of her own path. Notice, too, that the sutta is spoken to a woman, about a woman giver, and praises her by name. And notice what counts as the gift: not gold, not land. A meal, given and received every day.
screen: `SHE GIVES LIFE AND BEAUTY.` · `HAPPINESS AND STRENGTH.` · `THE GIFT COMES BACK.` · then, large: `FOOD IS LIFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last meal someone made or bought for you, and let yourself feel it again: life, color, comfort, strength. Then think of someone you could feed, a housemate, a coworker, a neighbor, a person on the corner, a food bank shelf. Picture handing it over, a sandwich, a cup of tea, nothing grand, with the four things going with it.
dana. The Pali and Sanskrit word for giving, from the Buddha's words to Suppavasa: giving food gives life, beauty, happiness and strength, and the giver shares in all four. Today's word.
Your line: a gift that comes back. A plate of rice carries more than rice. Day six hundred sixty-seven, done.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries, lay Buddhists offer food to monks on the morning alms round or at the temple, and giving food is one of the ways lay Buddhists practice dana, generosity.
